sources.title: BRAIN 2.0: From Cells to Circuits, Toward Cures
sources.publicationDate: 2019 (report presented to NIH ACD on June 14, 2019; final reports presented on October 21, 2019, per archived page)
sources.locator: Archived report page (Wayback 20231031143630): intro and Executive Summary, Priority Area 4/5 vision paragraph
sources.excerpt: we envision widespread adoption of integrated neurotechnologies that enable scientists to modulate activity throughout the brain
sources.paraphrase: The ACD BRAIN Initiative Working Group 2.0 report reviews BRAIN Initiative progress against BRAIN 2025 and lays out priorities for new neurotechnology for recording and modulating brain circuits, plus neuroethics. It is a neuroscience and neurotechnology research plan, not a biomedical engineering grand-challenge list.
sources.limitations: The cited URL slug never hosted the document as far as the archive shows. The real report is a 2019 neuroscience strategy. It does not support organ regeneration, biomaterials, imaging, blood substitutes or most other BME milestones, and it does not claim zero foreign-body response or decades-stable interfaces. The braininitiative.nih.gov site now redirects to nih.gov/brain (path /brain/about/vision/brain-20-cells-circuits-toward-cures), which returned 403 to the tools, so the text was read from the Wayback copy.
sources.evidenceForVerdict: curl -I on the cited URL gave 301 to nih.gov/brain (403). No CDX capture of /strategic-planning/brain-2.0, and /strategic-planning itself was archived as 404 (20220308, 20230405). A web search found the real BRAIN 2.0 report at /vision/nih-brain-initiative-reports/brain-20-report-cells-circuits-toward-cures. Its old URL now 302-redirects to https://www.nih.gov/brain/about/vision/brain-20-cells-circuits-toward-cures. Read the Wayback capture of 2023-10-31 (title confirmed). The document is real; the cited URL looks like a guessed path.

sources.title: Foreign body response to synthetic polymer biomaterials and the role of adaptive immunity
sources.excerpt: Implanted biomaterials elicit a series of distinct immune and repair-like responses that are collectively known as the foreign body reaction
sources.paraphrase: This Yale review says implanted synthetic polymers trigger a foreign body reaction: macrophages fuse into giant cells and the implant is encapsulated in a dense, largely avascular collagen capsule. It adds that adaptive immune cells (T and B cells) also take part, though their exact roles remain unclear.
sources.limitations: The PMC HTML was blocked, and only the abstract was read. The review documents the problem; it does not show a non-immunogenic universal material.
sources.evidenceForVerdict: esummary and efetch confirm the title, date, journal and DOI.

sources.excerpt: a novel design and a proof-of-concept validation of a mobile skin bioprinting system

sources.title: Real-Time Prediction of Lumbar Spine Stress and Displacement Using a Proof-of-Concept Digital Twin Biomechanical Model
sources.excerpt: To develop a proof-of-concept digital twin framework for real-time prediction and visualization of lumbar spine biomechanics
sources.paraphrase: A hybrid multibody-dynamics and finite-element framework with Kriging surrogates predicted lumbar spine stress and displacement in real time, for native and fused (TLIF with pedicle screw) spines. Mean absolute errors were at most 0.5% (native) and 0.2% (postoperative) against full simulations, and intradiscal pressures were within literature ranges.
sources.limitations: This is a numerical verification for one spinal segment region and is not clinically validated. It is far from a whole-body, continuously updated patient twin.
sources.evidenceForVerdict: Live PubMed page and efetch abstract are readable. The prior 'search-only' status is upgraded.
